name: Campanula
lede: Campanula is the botanical name of the bellflowers, borrowed for a deep violet-blue; the books agree on the flower and disagree on whether the color leans blue or purple.

sections.title: A flower's name
sections.body:
*Campanula* is the genus of the bellflowers, and the color is named for their petals [1][2]. Paterson's dictionary defines it as a violetish blue and credits its use to the art theorist Charles Blanc, who lived from 1813 to 1882 [3]. In 1827 the Nuremberg dermatologist Heinrich Eichhorn used the flower the same way in a list of skin colors, which includes the "purple of a campanula" [4].

So the books disagree on the hue. Paterson reads it as a blue with a violet tint [3]. Baty files it among the purples, as number 39 in a chart of blues and purples, next to [[pansy-purple]] [1]. The swatch here sits between the two, a deep violet that is bluer than [[purple]] and redder than [[violet-blue]] [5].

sections.title: One color in three kingdoms
sections.body:
Baty's chart pairs each color with a specimen from the animal, plant and mineral worlds [2]. For Campanula Purple the specimens are the wings of the Camberwell Beauty butterfly from a book of 1840, the petals of a peach-leaved bellflower from Jane Loudon's flower-garden book of 1849, and a piece of fluorite from Kurr's *Mineral Kingdom* of 1859 [2]. The plate's heading calls the flower the Canterbury bell, and gives its botanical name as *Campanula persicifolia* [2].

The pairing is the point of such charts: a reader could name a color by holding a real thing against it. A bellflower, a butterfly wing and a lump of purple fluorite are meant to be the same color to the eye [2].

sections.title: The swatch and its date
sections.body:
The swatch is the chip from Maerz and Paul's color dictionary of 1930, plate 42, row J, column 10 [5]. That book gives 1918 as the first recorded use, which is late for the name, since Eichhorn's flower comparison was in print in 1827 [5][4]. The 1918 date records what Maerz and Paul found in use, not when the word began [5].

The nearest named color in our data is [[purple]], at a distance of 5.3 on the CIEDE2000 scale [5]. The argument between Paterson and Baty is about which side of that line the flower falls on [3][1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
This is a rare painted color. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, only 2 contain a color within six units of the swatch that covers at least five per cent of the canvas [6]. One is [[painter:john-singer-sargent|Sargent]]'s *[[painting:commons-Q131754092|Bedouins]]* of 1905, at about 11 per cent of the picture [6]. The other is a portrait by Gervase Spencer of 1760, at about 6 per cent [6].

Two hits is too few to say anything about a century or a painter. As always these are photographs of varnished paintings, so the match is a screen color, not a pigment test [6].
